model_solution:
1. Pay {2} and activate **Indulgent Aristocrat**, sacrificing the battlefield **Sacred Cat**. Put a +1/+1 counter on each Vampire. Vampire Cutthroat and Indulgent Aristocrat are now 2/2.
2. Pay {W} to embalm Sacred Cat, creating a 1/1 Sacred Cat Zombie token.
3. Attack the opponent with **Vampire Cutthroat** and **Indulgent Aristocrat**.
4. Vampire Cutthroat cannot be blocked: it currently has power 2, while Bruna and both Renegade Ralliers have greater power, so skulk forbids them from blocking it.
5. After blockers are declared, pay {2} and activate Indulgent Aristocrat again, sacrificing the embalmed Cat token. Both Vampires become 3/3. Pumping Vampire Cutthroat now does not allow the opponent to revise their blocks.
6. Resolve combat damage. Vampire Cutthroat deals 3 damage to the opponent. Indulgent Aristocrat deals 3 damage either to the opponent or to its blocker(s). Because both have lifelink, you gain 6 life regardless of blocks, going from 21 to 27. The opponent is at 0 or less but remains in the game because of Gideon’s emblem.
7. In your second main phase, pay {1} and activate **Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim’s** first ability, sacrificing the now-3/3 Vampire Cutthroat. Gain 3 life, going to 30—ten above the normal starting life total.
8. Cast the **Sacred Cat** from your hand for {W}.
9. Pay {1}{W}{B} and activate Ayli’s second ability, sacrificing that Sacred Cat and targeting **Gideon of the Trials**. Exile Gideon.
10. The opponent no longer controls a Gideon planeswalker, so the emblem no longer prevents them from losing. Since their life total is 0 or less, they lose as a state-based action.

Total mana spent: {10}.

Puzzle conventions:
Winning
Unless otherwise stated, you must win the puzzle by inflicting lethal damage to your opponent before the turn ends. This can be as late as during the cleanup step if necessary. Your solution must work for all possible outcomes, such as your opponent’s actions and blocking decisions (see below.)
Phase
Unless otherwise stated, you begin each puzzle at the beginning of your first main phase. You have already drawn a card and gone past upkeep triggers. You have not yet played a land, cast any spells, activated any abilities of permanents on the battlefield, or attacked.
Your Opponent’s Resources / Actions
Unless otherwise stated, your opponent has no cards in hand and no other permanents in play (including no lands – despite the lack of realism there.) This means the only actions you need to consider are activated abilities with no mana cost. Most puzzles with opponent actions will offer more information on this.
Blocking
You cannot assume that your opponent will block a certain way, unless they are somehow forced to. Your solution must satisfy all possible blocking scenarios, even ones that would seem strange in a regular game, and always deal lethal in order to be correct.
Dice
Sometimes you will see six-sided dice placed on cards. These are meant to indicate counters, of whatever type is most reasonable to be there. On most creatures they will be +1/+1 counters, on most artifacts and lands they will be charge counters, and on most Planeswalkers they will be loyalty counters.
If the card specifies a type of counter itself, however (like Icatian Javelineers or Raging Ravine), that will dictate which type it is. 
For -1/-1 counters, we will use a separate graphic to avoid confusion.
Zones
Unless otherwise stated, all zones not displayed are empty. Neither you nor your opponent have cards in graveyards or in exile.
Cards Drawn from Libraries
In any puzzle in which either player might draw cards or otherwise access their library, the puzzle will stipulate some known or assumed information about the library.
Most commonly, this will be a statement that you should assume that the cards remaining in libraries are to be assumed to be irrelevant to the puzzle.
Your Life
Occasionally, your own life total might appear to matter – for cards like Anguished Unmaking, for example. If we require you to consider your own life total in a puzzle, it will be displayed.
If your life total is not shown, you may assume it is irrelevant and effectively infinite.

</solution>

Your line must be legal under the rules and must win against all possible opponent responses and blocking decisions.

4842:702.118. Skulk
4844:702.118a Skulk is an evasion ability.
4846:702.118b A creature with skulk can’t be blocked by creatures with greater power. (See rule 509, “Declare Blockers Step.”)
4848:702.118c Multiple instances of skulk on the same creature are redundant.
8831:A keyword ability that restricts how a creature may be blocked. See rule 702.118, “Skulk.”

1107:120.3f Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source’s controller to gain that much life, in addition to the damage’s other results.
4018:702.15b Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source’s controller, or its owner if it has no controller, to gain that much life (in addition to any other results that damage causes). See rule 120.3.

1073:119.6. If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game as a state-based action. See rule 704.
5464:704.5a If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game.
5514:704.6a In a Two-Headed Giant game, if a team has 0 or less life, that team loses the game. See rule 810, “Two-Headed Giant Variant.”
5527:Example: You control Lich’s Mirror, which says “If you would lose the game, instead shuffle your hand, your graveyard, and all permanents you own into your library, then draw seven cards and your life total becomes 20.” There’s one card in your library and your life total is 1. A spell causes you to draw two cards and lose 2 life. The next time state-based actions are checked, you’d lose the game due to rule 704.5a and rule 704.5b. Instead, Lich’s Mirror replaces that game loss and you keep playing.
6704:Example: In a Two-Headed Giant game, a player controls Transcendence, which reads, in part, “You don’t lose the game for having 0 or less life.” If that player’s team’s life total is 0 or less, that team doesn’t lose the game.

If the number of requirements that are being obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number of requirements that could be obeyed without disobeying any restrictions, the declaration of blockers is illegal. A creature remains blocked even if all the creatures blocking it are removed from combat.
2372:509.3c An ability that reads “Whenever [a creature] becomes blocked, . . .” generally triggers only once each combat for that creature, even if it’s blocked by multiple creatures. It will trigger if that creature becomes blocked by at least one creature declared as a blocker. It will also trigger if that creature becomes blocked by an effect or by a creature that’s put onto the battlefield as a blocker, but only if the attacking creature was an unblocked creature at that time. 8707:An effect that forces one or more creatures to attack or block. See rules 508.1d and 509.1c.
8719:An effect that precludes one or more creatures from attacking or blocking. See rules 508.1c and 509.1b.

2393:510.1a Each attacking creature and each blocking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power. Creatures that would assign 0 or less damage this way don’t assign combat damage at all.
2397:510.1c A blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it. If no creatures are currently blocking it (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If two or more creatures are blocking it, it assigns its combat damage to those creatures divided as its controller chooses among them.
4127:702.22j During the combat damage step, if an attacking creature is being blocked by a creature with banding, or by both a [quality] creature with “bands with other [quality]” and another [quality] creature, the defending player (rather than the active player) chooses how the attacking creature’s damage is assigned. That player can divide that creature’s combat damage as they choose among any creatures blocking it. This is an exception to the procedure described in rule 510.1c.
7530:Previously, if a creature blocks or becomes blocked by multiple creatures, the creature’s controller would be required to choose an order in which it would assign combat damage to the creatures blocking or blocked by it. Now, its controller no longer needs to assign an order, and simply divides its combat damage as they choose among all creatures it’s blocking or blocked by. See rules 510.1c-d.
